title: Oral arguments on BSKE postponement urged anew
summary: Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal has again asked the Supreme Court to hear oral arguments on his pending motion for partial reconsideration challenging the constitutionality of the law postponing…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal has again asked the Supreme Court (SC) to hear oral arguments on his pending motion for partial reconsideration challenging the constitutionality of the law postponing the November 2026 barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE).

In a manifestation with motion for clarification and reiterative motion for oral arguments filed on Nov. 18, Macalintal disputed the position of Commission on Elections (Comelec) Chairman George Garcia that Congress would have to pass a new law setting the election date should the SC reverse its earlier ruling upholding Republic Act 12326.
Macalintal argued that the Comelec already has the authority to reschedule and conduct the postponed elections without waiting for another legislative enactment.

He said Sections 5 and 6 of the Omnibus Election Code, read alongside the poll body’s constitutional mandate to administer election laws, require the Comelec to schedule a postponed or failed election within 30 days after the cause of the postponement ceases to exist.

Under this interpretation, a final SC ruling invalidating RA 12326 or its election-deferral provisions would remove the legal obstacle preventing the elections from proceeding, triggering the 30-day period for the Comelec to set the polls.

Macalintal said the poll body would therefore be mandated to act once the reversal becomes final and executory. He cited a hypothetical scenario in which the SC decision becomes final on Jan. 1, 2027, arguing that the Comelec would have 30 days from that date to hold the elections.

He also warned that requiring Congress to pass another law after the SC invalidates the postponement measure would undermine judicial review and allow the legislature to exercise continuing control over the election schedule.
Requiring another legislative enactment, he said, would effectively allow Congress to repeatedly postpone the BSKE even after the Supreme Court had ruled against the legality of its previous action.

“Indeed, under such a posture, Congress would become a super-powerful agency: even if its actions are declared invalid, it would still be the very body to enact a law implementing the election it sought to postpone in its invalid legislation,” Macalintal said in his pleading.

He added that subjecting an election ordered by the court to congressional approval could leave voters without recourse, particularly if a postponement measure is enacted only days before the scheduled polls.

Macalintal also cited the 2025 Supreme Court ruling in Hagedorn v. House of Representatives, which held that the Comelec need not wait for a resolution from the House of Representatives before calling a special election to fill a legislative vacancy.

In that case, the SC recognized that conducting a special election within 60 days of a vacancy is a primary power and duty of the Comelec, and that waiting for a formal legislative declaration could cause unnecessary delays.

Macalintal said the same principle should apply to the BSKE, arguing that the Comelec could immediately schedule and conduct the elections once the statutory basis for their postponement is struck down.
